source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psych Bull 138(6):1085-1108
finding: Founding statement of the theory theory in its Bayesian form. Intuitive theories have three marks: structure (coherent, abstract, causal, with hidden entities and a hierarchy of framework and specific theories), function (prediction, interpretation of evidence, counterfactuals and interventions) and dynamics (change in light of evidence, broadly, through intermediate conceptions).
numbers: No new data. Cites about 20 years of work (Carey 1985; Gopnik 1988; Gopnik & Meltzoff 1997; Wellman 1990; Keil 1989).
quote: theories change in the light of new evidence, and they do so in a rational way
limits: Review, so claims about children rest on the cited studies. Authors admit the older theory theory had a central theoretical vagueness about representations and learning mechanisms. Nativist rivals (core knowledge, modules; Spelke, Carey) dispute 'theories all the way down'.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for what REVISE should do: keep a structured causal hypothesis, let evidence change it, allow intermediate hypotheses, allow change in the higher-level principles, not just local details.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psych Bull 138(6):1085-1108
finding: Formal core: causal Bayes nets (Pearl; Spirtes, Glymour, Scheines) represent theories; hierarchical Bayes nets represent framework theories above specific ones; Bayesian updating explains how evidence changes belief. Interventions are graph surgery, and counterfactuals use the same machinery.
numbers: Example probabilistic claim: a block that sets off a machine 2 of 3 times is judged more causally effective than one that works 2 of 6 times (Kushnir et al 2005, as reported here).
limits: Normative framework. Children are shown to match it only in simple, small causal systems (2 to 4 variables, mostly deterministic).
agent_relevance: Supports a design where the model holds an explicit hypothesis set with weights and updates it from a counted check result, not from free text.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psych Bull 138(6):1085-1108
finding: Answer to the search problem: a learner cannot test all hypotheses, so it samples. Sample from the current hypothesis distribution, test the sample against evidence, update, sample again. Variants take a likely hypothesis and mutate it into similar neighbours. Statisticians can show this step-by-step process converges to the full Bayesian answer in the long run.
numbers: No numbers. Described as Monte Carlo style search (Robert and Casella 1999 cited).
limits: Convergence is a long-run result. The paper gives no estimate of how many steps children need. The link from child behaviour to a specific algorithm (MCMC, particle filter) is argued, not shown.
agent_relevance: Template for S5 conjecture refinement: keep several live hypotheses, test a sampled one, mutate the best, re-weight. Variability among attempts is a feature, not noise.

source: Denison, Bonawitz, Gopnik, Griffiths (2010) Preschoolers sample from probability distributions, as described in Gopnik & Wellman 2012
finding: 4-year-olds were told a red or blue chip in a machine made it go, then guessed the colour of a hidden chip several times. Guesses matched the chance of each colour (probability matching), not always the most likely colour. In a two-bag version they matched the chance that each colour ended up in the machine, not the raw chip counts.
numbers: 80 red / 20 blue bag: children chose red about 80% of the time and blue about 20%. 60/40 bag: children shifted accordingly. Two-bag condition (one bag 2 blue; one bag 14 red + 6 blue): blue was more likely in the machine than red, and children's answers followed that.
limits: Read only as summarised in Gopnik & Wellman 2012, not the original. Probability matching is also what a noisy responder does; the two-bag condition rules out plain frequency matching, but sample sizes were not in the summary.
agent_relevance: Shows 'try low probability hypotheses some of the time' is a human-like policy. Gives a case for sampling several attempts in proportion to confidence rather than always taking the top one.

source: Gopnik, Sobel, Schulz, Glymour (2001) Causal learning mechanisms in very young children. Dev Psych 37:620-629 (as described in Gopnik & Wellman 2012 and McClelland & Thompson 2007)
finding: Founding blicket detector study. A machine lights and plays music for some objects (blickets). After seeing patterns of single and joint trials, 2-, 3- and 4-year-olds picked the right blocks and then acted correctly to make the machine go or stop (add only A; remove only A).
numbers: One-cause task: A+ once, B- once, AB+ twice; normative answer A is a blicket, B is not. Two-cause task: A+ 3, B+ 2, B- 1; both are blickets. 4-year-olds called the 67%-effective object a blicket 16% of the time (one-cause) and 78% (two-cause); 3-year-olds 66% and 85% (figures from McClelland & Thompson 2007).
limits: Original not read: the figshare copy was a scanned PDF with no text layer. Numbers come from a secondary account. Three-year-olds departed from the normative answer in the one-cause task.
agent_relevance: Choosing A not B after inference is the agent's next step: use the revised hypothesis to pick the next test or action.

source: McClelland & Thompson (2007) Using domain-general principles to explain children's causal reasoning abilities. Developmental Science 10(3):333-356
finding: Main competing model. A standard connectionist network (back-propagation, interleaved presentation, weight decay) trained on the same blicket events reproduced children's one-cause, two-cause and screening-off results and gave graded backward-blocking estimates, with no causal-specific machinery.
numbers: Network matched children's blicket rate for B in common vs rare blicket contexts, with close numerical correspondence in the backward blocking condition. After AB+ alone, children called B a blicket more often than the network did. Quoted children's data: one-cause 67% object, 4-year-olds 16% yes, 3-year-olds 66% yes.
quote: without appealing to inherent principles or mechanisms specialized for causal as opposed to other forms of reasoning
limits: Needs interleaved training. Sequential training with plain Rescorla-Wagner fails on backward blocking, so the model re-presents earlier events. Authors do not claim children lack Bayes nets, only that domain-general learning suffices for these data.
agent_relevance: A result that looks like Bayesian hypothesis revision can be reproduced by a plain learner. For our agent, pass rate on a blicket-style task alone does not show a theory-like process.

source: Schulz, Gopnik, Glymour (2007) Preschool children learn causal structure from conditional interventions. Developmental Science 10:322-332 (author manuscript submitted 2004)
finding: Experiment 1 (gear toy). Preschoolers saw combinations of interventions on a switch and two gears and had to say which gear was causal. They used the logic of conditional interventions (fix other variables, vary one) to tell cause from effect, where mechanism, time-order and association cues gave no help.
numbers: Exp 1: 80 children, mean age 4;6 (40-64 months). Test condition n=25: 84% correct on trial 1, 76% on trial 2, 64% correct on both (binomial p<.025). Three controls n=18 each: movement 33% on both trials, still 6%, contrast 22%; test beat controls by chi-square (3.94, 14.95, 7.34; N=43 each).
quote: children were able to use information from interventions to make causal inferences when relevant differential mechanism information and spatiotemporal information was not available
limits: Small groups; deterministic, generative, 2 to 3 variable systems only. Authors say children's own spontaneous interventions were not yet tested. Exp 4 (given structure, predict evidence): only 12% right on all four predictions, though above chance.
agent_relevance: A clean rule that works: fix other factors, then change one. This is a G3 style check (test on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Schulz, Gopnik, Glymour (2007) Experiments 2 and 3
finding: Children chose among four possible gear structures (two chains, common effect, conjunction) after switch-and-gear interventions, and picked the correct structure for the chain, common-effect and conjunction cases. Without evidence about the switch they fell to chance.
numbers: Exp 2 group A: 60% correct on both trials (n=20, p<.001). Exp 2 group without switch evidence: 37% (chain) and 50% (conjunction) correct, no better than chance (n=16). Exp 3: common effect 71% correct, conjunction 86% correct (n=14 each); 57% right on both trials (p<.001).
limits: Same small-n, deterministic limits. Chance is 25 to 33% depending on choice set. Custom electronic toy.
agent_relevance: The control variable has to be handled for the inference to go through: the agent should not revise from a test that left a confound free.

source: Sobel, Yoachim, Gopnik, Meltzoff, Blumenthal (2007) The blicket within: preschoolers' inferences about insides and causes. J Cognition & Development 8(2):159-182
finding: 4-year-olds, unlike 3-year-olds, linked an artifact's hidden internal part to its causal power rather than to its outside look, when the link was framed as causal not associative.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=64): 61% placed the block with the causally efficacious insert on the detector (one-tailed p=.05; not significant two-tailed, p<.10); 83% identified the right insert as the blicket. Exp 4: 3-year-olds chose the internally similar object 31% (causal) and 19% (association); 4-year-olds 72% (causal) and 17% (association). ANOVA age F(1,60)=5.91, condition F(1,60)=17.48, interaction F(1,60)=6.89.
limits: Directional test chosen from pilot data; the p=.05 result in Exp 1 does not hold two-tailed. Side bias to the right-hand block (chi-square 28.90). Small groups (n=16 per cell).
agent_relevance: Hidden-cause reasoning is a developmental step and depends on a causal frame. Prompting for a hidden part that explains the data may need to be worded causally, not associatively.

source: Weisberg, Choi, Sobel (2020) Of blickets, butterflies, and baby dinosaurs: children's diagnostic reasoning across domains. Front Psychol 11:2210
finding: Replicates the slow (age 5 to 8) development of diagnostic, backward causal inference with blickets and extends it to a matched biological butterfly task. Content of the task changes whether the capacity shows.
numbers: Exp 1 N=242 children aged 4-10 (116 blicket, 126 butterfly). 4-5 and 6-7 year-olds at chance (33% with 3 choices, all p>.19); 8-10 year-olds above chance (blicket p=.007, butterfly p<.001). Exp 2 N=112 replicated. Exp 3 N=110: a biological category-membership version was hard. Age effect Wald chi2(1)=10.56, p=.001; no condition effect.
limits: Boundary on the 'children as scientists' claim: diagnostic inference over several uncertain causes is late. Authors suggest content can hide an earlier capacity.
agent_relevance: Task framing and content change whether revision skill shows. Test revision on several domains before claiming it.

source: Benton & Rakison (c. 2014; year not confirmed) Causal reasoning in infants and adults: revisiting backwards-blocking. CogSci proceedings
finding: Failed or partial replication of backward blocking. 6-month-old infants showed no looking-time difference across four test events. Adults replicated screening-off but did not lower B's rating after A+ (the backward-blocking trial).
numbers: Exp 1: 19 infants (about 6 months); looking time to A+, A-, B+, B- did not differ, F(3,54)=0.28, p=.84; B+ 9.58 s vs B- 11.17 s, t(5)=0.39, p=.72. Exp 2: 60 adults; A's rating rose from M=50.83 to 96.25 (t(59)=-19.73, p<.006); B's rating did not differ pre vs post after backward blocking.
limits: Year of the proceedings not confirmed in the text read. Adults may split into associative and backward-blocking reasoners (a 'causal gradient'). Sobel & Kirkham (2006, 2007) report the opposing infant result.
agent_relevance: Strong sign that Bayesian explaining away is not universal. Do not assume the model will down-weight B after A alone explains the data; check it by counted rule.

source: Gopnik, O'Grady, Lucas, Griffiths et al. (2017) Changes in cognitive flexibility and hypothesis search across human life history from childhood to adolescence to adulthood. PNAS 114(30):7892-7899
finding: Younger learners adopt an unusual, evidence-supported hypothesis more often than older learners in the blicket task. Adolescents and adults stick to the default 'or' rule. In a social task the pattern is an inverted U, with adolescents most flexible.
numbers: Exp 1 (blicket, conjunctive condition), labelled object D a blicket: 4-year-olds 92%, 6-7 yr 56% (n=90), 9-11 yr 60% (n=90), 12-14 yr 28% (n=86), adults 25%. Chose multiple objects: 4-yr 84%, 6-7 yr 53%, 9-11 yr 63%. Exp 2 situation-attribution baseline score: 4 yr 0.93, 6 yr 0.43, 9-11 yr 0.55, 12-14 yr 0.24, adults 0.38.
quote: Adults applied the default disjunctive rule in the ambiguous case even when the earlier evidence weighed against it.
limits: 4-year-old and adult data come from earlier papers (Lucas 2014; Seiver 2013), so groups were not tested in one design. Read through a page-summary tool; the last 9,000 characters were not read. Author list is abbreviated here.
agent_relevance: Priors can block revision. Matches G1 and the idea that a strong prior is overcome only by counted evidence; suggests keeping a broad hypothesis space instead of locking to the default early.

source: Lucas, Bridgers, Griffiths, Gopnik (2014) When children are better (or at least more open-minded) learners than adults. Cognition 131:284-299 (as reported in Gopnik et al 2017)
finding: Original conjunctive-versus-disjunctive blicket study. After evidence for an unusual conjunctive rule, 4-year-olds applied it to ambiguous new blocks more than adults.
numbers: Summary figures only, from the 2017 paper: 4-year-olds 92% called the test object a blicket under the conjunctive rule versus adults 25%.
limits: Original not opened. Later work reports adults improve with active exploration (Samiei et al). Wente et al 2019 found the adult handicap across cultures (as cited in Samiei).
agent_relevance: Learning the rule type (overhypothesis) is a separate step from identifying objects.

source: Schulz & Bonawitz (2007) Serious fun; Cook, Goodman, Schulz (2011) Where science starts (as described in Gopnik & Wellman 2012)
finding: Preschoolers explore more when evidence is ambiguous. With a two-lever toy, a confounded demonstration led 3- and 4-year-olds to play with the old toy rather than a new simple toy; a clear demonstration did not. Cook et al. found children pick informative tests given their background knowledge.
numbers: Numbers not given in the review; only the direction (more exploration of the old toy in the confounded condition, and later evidence they had worked out the structure).
limits: Originals not opened. Chen & Klahr 1999 and Kuhn found older children and adults design controlled experiments poorly when asked explicitly, a limit to the child-as-scientist analogy.
agent_relevance: Rule: when the evidence is confounded, spend the next test on the ambiguous item; once clear, move on. A counted ambiguity check.

source: Bonawitz, Shafto, Gweon, Goodman, Spelke, Schulz (2011) The double-edged sword of pedagogy (as described in Gopnik & Wellman 2012)
finding: A toy had many hidden functions. When a demonstrator said she was showing how it works, children copied the one action and explored less. When she activated it by accident, children explored and found more functions.
numbers: No numbers in the review text.
limits: Original not opened. The cost of a teacher's framing is narrower search.
agent_relevance: A confident framing in a prompt ('here is how it works') may cut the agent's own exploration of alternatives. Keep an unprompted exploration pass.

source: Gweon & Schulz (2011) 16-month-olds rationally infer causes of failed actions. Science 332:1524 (as described in Gopnik & Wellman 2012)
finding: Infants as young as 16 months inferred from evidence whether a failure was due to them or to the toy, and chose to try again or hand the toy to someone else.
numbers: Not given in the review. The original paper could not be retrieved this session (download returned a 404 page).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Telling 'my attempt failed' from 'the world failed' is the same split as a bug in the method versus a bug in the hypothesis.

source: Xu & Garcia (2008) Intuitive statistics by 8-month-old infants; Kushnir, Xu, Wellman (2010) Young children use statistical sampling to infer the preferences of other people (as described in GW 2012)
finding: Infants treat a sample as random from a population (look longer when a mostly-red sample comes from a mostly-white box). By 20 months a non-random sample (frogs taken from a box of mostly ducks) is read as a preference and the child hands over frogs; a random-looking sample is not.
numbers: Box 80/20 white/red ping-pong balls (Xu & Garcia, 8-month-olds). Kushnir 2010: 20-month-olds gave frogs when sampled from a mostly-duck box; frog or duck about equally when from a mostly-frog box.
limits: Cell counts not reported in the review. Originals not opened. Infant looking-time measures carry known replication risk.
agent_relevance: How the evidence was sampled changes what it means. The same output counts differently if the source selected it.

source: Bonawitz, Ferranti, Saxe, Gopnik, Meltzoff, Woodward, Schulz (2010) Just do it? Children's causal inference from human action versus spontaneous events (as described in GW 2012)
finding: 4-year-olds, but not 2-year-olds, acted on a box to make a toy plane spin after seeing the boxes interact with no person involved. 2-year-olds did so only when a person had made the same events happen.
numbers: Direction only. Meltzoff et al. (in press) confirmed with 24-month-olds, 3- and 4-year-olds, with added controls.
limits: Original not opened. A boundary: young children's causal inference is tied to agent actions.
agent_relevance: Evidence from an agent's action is treated as more informative than passive correlation. Parallel to tool output versus self-generated claims.

source: Liu et al. (2007) and Siegler (1995, 2007) as discussed in Gopnik & Wellman 2012: variability in theory change
finding: About 50 preschoolers each did 20 to 30 false-belief tasks. At group level most seemed consistent, but every child mixed right and wrong answers. Variability may be part of how theories change.
numbers: 65% passed more than 75% of the tasks; about 30% passed fewer than 25%; three children in the middle. Every child gave a mix of realist and false-belief answers.
limits: As reported in the review; original not opened. Cuts against clean stage views (Piaget) and favours gradual shift of probabilities.
agent_relevance: Expect mixed outputs mid-revision. A sharp switch in aggregate may be gradual per trial; one wrong answer is not proof of no revision.

source: Kosoy, Liu, Collins, Chan, Hamrick, Ke, Huang, Kaufmann, Canny, Gopnik (2022) Learning causal overhypotheses through exploration in children and computational models. CLeaR / PMLR 140
finding: Online blicket-detector experiment with children plus information-gain-optimal agents. Children given the hypothesis space explored more effectively; children without it often stopped before the evidence could settle the question. Children used more steps than optimal agents.
numbers: N=85 children aged 4-5 (20-23 per condition), 2x2 conjunctive/disjunctive by hypothesis given/not given. Generated enough data to settle the rule: 71% given vs 32% not given (2-proportion z, p=0.002). About 12.4 actions in both structures. 17.7% and 17.5% tried the empty machine. About 66% tried a different order of the same objects in both conditions. Given: 14.07 actions in 178.65 s; not given: 10.58 actions in 195.38 s.
limits: Museum sample; children not forced to stop early. Authors state the reward children optimise is unknown. Agrees with Lucas 2014 that rule type changes little in how much children explore.
agent_relevance: Boundary on the child-as-scientist idea: without a defined hypothesis space most children fail to gather decisive evidence. Our agent needs an explicit hypothesis list before it tests.

source: Kosoy, Chan, Liu, Collins, Kaufmann, Huang, Hamrick, Canny, Ke, Gopnik (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses. arXiv 2206.08353
finding: Blicket-detector benchmark for machines. Deep RL agents (A2C, PPO2 with LSTM) and imitation models (Decision Transformer, behaviour cloning) generalised poorly to new causal overhypotheses. Early large language models were tried on a text version.
numbers: Table 1 examples: Decision Transformer with PPO2 layer-norm LSTM, mean reward 0.74 (sd 1.46), forced-choice accuracy 0.64; behaviour cloning forced-choice accuracies 0.55 to 0.68 (chance 0.5). GPT-3 and PaLM: four conditions with 1 to 2 runs each, mixed correct and wrong; several PaLM two-shot runs in conjunctive/not-given were wrong.
limits: Tiny LLM evaluation (a handful of prompts, GPT-3 and PaLM, 2022). Not a fair test of current models. RL agents were trained on the hypothesis set, so it does not test open-ended learning.
agent_relevance: Baseline showing learned policies do not generalise overhypothesis structure without an explicit mechanism. Later LLM work (Yiu 2023; Samiei 2026) updates this.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2023) Transmission versus truth, imitation versus innovation: what children can do that large language and language-and-vision models cannot (yet). Perspectives on Psychological Science
finding: LLMs match children at imitation (picking the associated object) but lag at innovation (picking a functionally relevant but superficially different tool). On a text blicket-detector task, LLMs did not produce the correct causal overhypotheses from the children's data.
numbers: Children 3-7 (n=42) and adults (n=30). Imitation: children 88.4%, adults 84.9%. Innovation: children 85.2%, adults 95.7%. LLM imitation: GPT-4 83.3%, gpt-3.5-turbo 73.1%, text-davinci 59.9%, Claude 69.9%, Flan-T5 74.8%. LLM innovation: GPT-4 75.9%, gpt-3.5-turbo 58.9%, davinci 8.87%, Claude 58.16%, Flan 45.7%.
limits: 2023 models, temperature 0, six option orders averaged. Perspective piece: the blicket result is stated without a table. Authors flag that GPT-4's gain might come from images or RLHF. No agentic loops.
agent_relevance: Knowing about causal relations is not discovering them. The schema should make the agent generate and run tests, not recall.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen, Lin, Shen, Richards, Gopnik, Precup (2025/2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration? CogSci 2026
finding: Active exploration helps adults on conjunctive blicket rules (the conjunctive handicap of passive learning shrinks). LLMs on the same task: some (gpt-5, deepseek-reasoner) reach near top-human on disjunctive rules, but explore less efficiently and keep a conjunctive gap.
numbers: 306 adults on Prolific: 102 active explorers, 102 passive observers, 102 passive proposers. Conjunctive object identification: active 0.69, passive observer 0.45, passive proposer 0.12; rule selection 0.82, 0.69, 0.57. Hypothesis space: 32 explanations. Models: gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, o4-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-chat, deepseek-reasoner.
limits: Exact model accuracies are in a figure and were not extracted. Proposers see another person's outcomes, so low scores may reflect plan-result mismatch. Adults only, no children.
agent_relevance: Generating and seeing your own test outcomes matters, and strong 2025 reasoning models can approach human active inference. Keep the loop closed: propose a test, run it, read the result.

source: Alderete, Benthall, Xu et al. (2026) Separable pathways for causal reasoning: how architectural scaffolding enables hypothesis-space restructuring in LLM agents. arXiv 2604.20039
finding: Extends the blicket detector to agents with a mid-run rule switch that forces them to revise the hypothesis space. Two scaffold parts act separately: a context graph (typed state machine for exploration) improves reasoning quality; dynamic behaviours (monitors that expand the hypothesis space on contradicting evidence) prevent premature commitment.
numbers: 1,085 trials, Claude Sonnet 4.5 as reasoning model (Haiku for monitors). Run 08 conjunctive post-switch: reasoning accuracy Base 73.3% (22/30), context graph 93.9% (31/33) (+20.6 pp, Fisher p=0.038, h=0.59), plus monitors 95.3% (41/43). Context graph accounts for 94% of the gain. Exactly-N trap: context graph 28.0% (14/50) vs plus monitors 6.0% (3/50), p=0.003. Combined switch-at-3 (n=110 per agent) raw accuracy Base 87.3%, CG 77.3%, CG+DB 89.1%. Monitor sensitivity 100% across five datasets.
limits: Preprint, single lab, one model family. CG numerically below Base on raw accuracy (77.3 vs 87.3%, not significant) because of the exactly-N trap.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of our S5. Design principle: separate 'detect that the hypothesis space is wrong' (code monitor) from 'reason well inside it' (structured exploration). Supports G1 and G2.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psych Bull 138(6):1085-1108 (hierarchical learning section)
finding: Four-year-olds can learn abstract higher-order rules about a causal system before knowing specifics: they extended a disjunctive or conjunctive rule to new blocks (Lucas et al., in press), and know biological and artifact objects have different insides without knowing what the insides are (Gelman & Wellman 1991).
numbers: Children say eggs have blood and guts and piggy banks have gears: framework knowledge exists with wrong details.
limits: The review notes the framework-level claim rests on a small set of studies.
agent_relevance: Revise at two levels: the specific hypothesis and the rule type that generates hypotheses. Let a high-level class of rules carry over to new items.

source: Seiver, Gopnik, Goodman (2013) Did she jump because she was the big sister or because the trampoline was safe? (as described in Gopnik & Wellman 2012)
finding: 4-year-olds saw an action covary with a person or a situation and attributed it to a lasting trait of the person or to a feature of the toy, then predicted future behaviour.
numbers: Example frequencies only: Sally plays on the trampoline 3 of 4 times, Josie 1 of 4.
limits: Not opened. Gopnik 2017 later found adolescents better than adults and 6-year-olds on situation attribution, so the age pattern is not monotonic.
agent_relevance: Revision works for hidden-cause questions (person vs situation) as well as for physical machines.

source: Sobel, Tenenbaum, Gopnik (2004) Children's causal inferences from indirect evidence: backwards blocking and Bayesian reasoning in preschoolers. Cognitive Science 28:303-333 (as described in GW 2012, McC&T 2007, Benton & Rakison)
finding: Backward blocking: after AB+ and then A+, children judged B less likely to be a blicket than after AB+ alone; after AB+ then A-, B was clearly a blicket (screening off). The effect depended on how common blickets had been earlier, as a Bayesian model with a prior would predict.
numbers: Per McC&T Table 2: screening-off AB+ x2 then A- x1; backward blocking AB+ x2 then A+ x1 (B status undetermined). The 4-year-old group in Exp 1 was perfect on the screening-off condition; Exp 2 used one 4-year-old group (as quoted).
limits: Original not opened. Adults and 6-month-old infants did not show backward blocking in Benton & Rakison. Sobel & Kirkham (2006, 2007) reported it for infants.
agent_relevance: The key evidence for explaining away in children and the hardest to replicate. Treat as fragile.
